claims.text: Chemical short-range order, lattice strain, and dimensionality-induced magnetic anisotropy govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type nanoscale films or nanoribbons.
Pulsed laser deposition can control the composition of nanoscale alloy materials.
Pulsed laser deposition can controllably vary the composition of FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films or nanoribbons.
Thin-film fabrication can controllably vary lattice strain in FeMnNiGeSi-type thin films or nanoribbons.
Changing chemical composition changes chemical short-range order in the specified alloy system.
Chemical short-range order and lattice strain influence magnetic anisotropy in the specified low-dimensional alloy system.
Reducing the alloy to a nanoscale film or patterned nanoribbon changes its magnetic anisotropy.
Changes in magnetic anisotropy affect the magnetocaloric response of the specified alloy system.
Changes in magnetic anisotropy affect magnetic hysteresis in the specified alloy system.
The magnetocaloric response will vary when chemical composition and lattice strain are changed.
Magnetic hysteresis will vary when chemical composition and lattice strain are changed.
Controlled variation of composition and lattice strain could optimize magnetocaloric properties.
Heat-transfer rate limits the usable magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
Applied magnetic field and nanoscale dimensional constraints define operating boundaries for the response.
Failure of both magnetocaloric response and hysteresis to vary across changes in composition and lattice strain would falsify the hypothesis.
